newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul concerned about food distribution in N.Korea.
newsitem.headline: Seoul concerned about food distribution in N.Korea.

text.p: South Korea is concerned about food distribution in North Korea but will continue to respond to humanitarian appeals for more aid by United Nations agencies, a government spokesman said on Thursday.
"The government cannot help but be worried about the transparency in North Korea's food distribution," said Kang Ho-yang, spokesman of the National Unification Ministry.
Kang was commenting on remarks by U.S. congressmen just back from visiting North Korea that they believed some foreign food aid might have been diverted to the Stalinist state's military.

Seven members of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence told a joint news conference in Seoul on Wednesday they would seek measures to ensure future U.S. aid to North Korea would go directly to hungry people.

"I believe we would all agree that some food aid has probably ended up in the hands of the military and the other elites in the country and we are concerned about that," California lawmaker Jane Harman, one of the seven, said.

Kang said in a statement: "The government will step up efforts, in cooperation with the World Food Programme, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent and other international organisations, to secure transparency regarding food provided to the North."
A WFP spokesman said there was "no shred of evidence" that any of the U.N. body's aid was going astray.
"All the food that has been sent through WFP has gone to the beneficiaries," he said.
Kang told Reuters that Seoul would continue providing relief supplies if United Nations aid agencies appeal for help.
"The government's stand to continue humanitarian assistance to the North will remain unchanged," he said.
The United States and South Korea have led international efforts to provide food aid to North Korea, pledging $52 million and $16 million, respectively, so far this year through the WFP.
The South Korean Red Cross has promised an additional $20 million worth of food products to the North.
Kang said although Seoul will contribute to international food aid to the North, large-scale assistance would have to wait until Pyongyang begins substantive four-nation peace talks.

Officials of the two Koreas, the United States and China met in New York last week to set an agenda for the formal peace talks but failed to reach an agreement. They are due to try again on September 15 in New York.
The four-nation talks, proposed by Seoul and Washington last year, aim to set up a permanent peace mechanism on the Korean peninsula, the last flashpoint of the Cold War.
The two Koreas have been technically at war since the 1950-53 Korean War ended with an armistice agreement, and not with a peace treaty.
